utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, could we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours Teresa McHenry for the Prosecution, along with Mr. Cowles and Mr. Huber.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours I am Edina Residovic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, along with my colleague, professor Eugene O'Sullivan from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, I am Olujic appearing on behalf of Zdravko Mucic along with my colleague Mr. Duric. We're both attorneys from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, along with Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Houston Texas, I appear on behalf of Mr. Hasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Could morning, Your Honours I am Cynthia McMurrey, and along with my co-counsel Ms. Nancy Boler. We represent Esad Landzo and we're both from the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, you're still cross-examining, are you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I had finished my cross-examination, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Just a little bit, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, you're still under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask for your indulgence, during the appearances, I see that my statement has been omitted from the transcript, so could this be corrected, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think it will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And with your permission, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your statement this morning, your appearance wasn't reflected on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No, something else. In the course of yesterday's examination, when my learned colleague from the Prosecution was examining the witness, in view of the fact that my client was mentioned, may I also be allowed to examine the witness with two questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's all right, yes, you might. Please, Ms. Boler, let him ask his two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Examined by Olujic

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could morning, Mr. Turkovic. May I introduce myself, I am Olujic, Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. I shall be very brief Mr. Turkovic, with two questions that I have for you. Would it be correct to say that you saw Mr. Mucic in the Musala Collection Centre somewhere towards the end of August, 1992 when he was discharging people?

utterances.speaker: Senadin Turkovic.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Turkovic, would I be right in saying that you concluded on the superior position of Mr. Mucic on the basis of seeing him in Musala?

utterances.speaker: Senadin Turkovic.
utterances.text: That is right. When you see somebody signing the release papers for a large number of prisoners, then it is normal to conclude from that that he is in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further, Mr. Turkovic, am I right in saying that you have no personal knowledge about the actual position of Mr. Zdravko Mucic?

utterances.speaker: Senadin Turkovic.
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Boler, you can now proceed. Re-examined by Ms. Boler

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Turkovic.

utterances.speaker: Senadin Turkovic.
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a question or two. Do you recall speaking with Cynthia McMurrey when she came to interview witnesses in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: Senadin Turkovic.
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at that time, do you recall her asking you some questions about when Esad Landzo first came to be a guard at Musala?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask is she impeaching the witness or may I ask for how this arises out of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: My recollection is that there were some questions in cross-examination about when he arrived at Musala.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please confine your re-examination to matters which arose from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: My recollection was that it did arise from cross-examination. May I have a few minutes? I just have one last question. Do you recall telling Cynthia McMurrey that you weren't sure of the last day when Mr. Landzo arrived at Musala?

utterances.speaker: Senadin Turkovic.
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's still your testimony that you're not sure of that?

utterances.speaker: Senadin Turkovic.
utterances.text: Yes, if I may, I should like to elaborate a little on the way in which many people came to Musala. It could occur that five soldiers would come on the same day to volunteer and then the next day five or six would go away. So that at the beginning of the aggression, a group of people would spend five or six days there, sleeping there as well, whereas there was a turnover of people, people were coming and going everyday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for your answer, Mr. Turkovic. And I pass the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much Mr. Turkovic. You've been very helpful and we are grateful. This is the end of your examination, you're discharged now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have your next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour the Defence would like to call Dr. Alfredo Verde to the stand, please. (Witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly swear the

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Verde.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell the Court your full name please?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Alfredo Verde, and I am Italian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you had thought you were going to speak through an Italian interpreter?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I had, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're going to do your best to speak in English today?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, my English is not so good, but I will try to do my best for the Court and for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We appreciate that, thank you. You and I only metaphor the first time this Saturday, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me ask you -- Your Honours, I now have an English translation of Dr. Verde's curriculum vitae, which I would like to distribute to the Court. We didn't have it before. We just received it, so with the help of the usher, I would like to provide the Court with an English version of his curriculum vitae. And while we're doing that, I will go ahead and start. Dr. Verde, would you tell the Court about your educational experience?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. I had my classical studies when I finished at 18. I had -- I took a law degree and then I began again and took a psychology degree and I graduated in 19 -- I think 1986 -- '85, yes. But then I was already at the Criminological Institute of the University of Genoa. And after I began a Ph.D. and I had my PH.D. in 1990, yes. And that's the academic part of my curriculum vitae because I had yet still psychoanalytical training and I became a psychoanalyst. In Italy, we are called psychotherapist. It doesn't matter the school to whom you belong. And I am a psychoanalyst and now I am working at the -- now the name is Department of Legal Medicine, Medical Psychology and Criminal section of Psychiatry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's a new name?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, it changed one year, ago, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there you are also a member of a lot of -- well, you teach at the university --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, I teach most law students and to the school of specialisation, that means sort of specialisation of graduate, specialisation of clinical criminology. I teach forensic psychology, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're a member of a very elite group in the international community?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, I am a member of the Scientific Board of the International Society for criminology, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how many members from all over the world are there on the board?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, but we should be 25 at maximum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. At the University of Genoa, are you responsible for psycho-diagnostics in your department?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. The psycho-diagnostics section of the section of criminology, I am responsible, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I now have passed -- I want to say that we had a very quick interpretation of Dr. Verde's report too. So I will ask that the usher pass that out, because he has made just a few changes on it, just as far as the interpretation goes and these are all written in his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it's better that we go on with the job. If the Prosecution has any queries, they might raise it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he will review this report in a little bit. And some of these changes drastically change the meaning of the words because this was interpreted by someone who didn't have any experience in psychological testing and the terminology. So there is really only four or five changes, but I think they're instrumental in the Court understanding what he is going to be reviewing. And one of the first changes is that he is not director of the Institute of criminology, he is a researcher. So if the Court would just indulge me to pass these out, they are a few hand-written notes. So with the help of the usher, could I get him to distribute these, please. Now, I am not going to go into this report right now, but how did you come to -- to participate in this case?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Dr. Lagazzi spoke of it to me about one month ago, yes, one month ago. And he told me something of Landzo, but a very short description of his personality. We had a ten minutes talk about it and then he -- then I came to Holland to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, because he didn't really tell you any details about Mr. Landzo --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, no, in ten minutes, it's impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you went to perform the testing without any really preconceived ideas about --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, we call it blind testing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blind?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Blind testing, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is your clinical and forensic experience?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: In my position at the Criminological Section at the University of Genoa, I have conducted a lot of testing on criminal people. And I am doing tests since I am there, even before since my -- even before my graduation in psychology. I think since 1980. And doing such kind of tests, Rorschach and TAT. And I do some works for the Court, both in the criminal and in the civil fields. For example, child custody litigation and so on and an expert of both of the juvenile court and of the civil juvenile of Genoa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, you recently did some major studies on two very important Italian criminal cases. What were those?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Pietro Massa (Phon) and Luigi Zeppe (Phon). Pietro killed his parents and he had some particular personality disorder. And Luigi Zeppe was more severely psychotic and he killed two children in Foligno. It's a small Italian town in Umbria near Perugia. And I did some work both for the Defence team and for a more academic scientific point of view upon them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, in many of these cases that you participate in in Italy, someone else does the actual clinical testing and you're called in to interpret the results?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, because I have -- I do private practice too, so I am called by the Defence teams and I have to interpret the testing made by other psychologists in order to discuss the testing in court. For example, the Chiati (Phon) case was that. And we obtained a change in the evaluation by the Court of Appeal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know that everybody knows what the difference between a psychologist and a psychiatrist is?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there is just one major difference?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, I am not a physician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, not a physician.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I am not an MD.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to ask you before you tested Mr. Landzo, you didn't review any documents, did you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, not at all. After testing, I review some documents. Laggazi is one, Laggazi gave his paper to me for reading and I read Dr. Van Leuween reports, I think two, two reports. And nothing more until Sunday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Sunday we met together --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I presented you with the psychological testing of another doctor at that time.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Roorda de Man psychological report that I read just Sunday, Sunday night I finished it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell me what the results of her report were and how they differ from the report that you have completed?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: They are not very different from my results, but Roorda de Man, the first part of the report speaks about the interview she had with Landzo and describes his mental condition. Then she proceeded to do some psychological testing, mainly from the point of view of an evaluation of his mental level, intelligence. She did a lot of testing in that field and from the testing made -- it came out that Landzo was of average intelligence, maybe a little upon the average.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Above the average?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Above, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I am going to assist him if you don't mind because I know what he is trying to say?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, yes, my English. Yes, above the average. And then she -- I didn't know, she did not succeed in doing the projective part of the testing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why she didn't succeed in doing a successful projective testing on Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: She said that he was not interest in the things, he didn't -- he couldn't manage. And the projective testing presents the person with a lot of stimulus. The person cannot understand and cannot relate to anything, so maybe she said he was not interested in. And she tried to perform, to do the Rorschach, but Mr. Landzo didn't give any response, any answer. And she did the TAT and he gave some trivial response, some trivial answer that were not useful for arriving at some valid conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, so basically -- and what date was this test by Dr. Roorda de Man attempted?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Date, yes. Was November the 6th, 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this test, basically, where she left off --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me what the difference in her testing and your testing is?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, I have done this testing without seeing Roorda De Man's report and my test begins where Roorda de Man's ends. And the difference is I have been successful in doing the test, performing the task. And Mr. Landzo gave me a lot of answers. So it was possible to me to write a report evaluating the condition of his -- from a psychological point of view, evaluating the condition of his personality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these two reports, your report and Dr. Roorda de Man's report, are not consistent, they're just concentrating on two different areas?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, and my part can be seen as the continuation of Roorda de Man's work. And I succeeded finished in what she didn't succeed because given the condition of the patient, if I can call him so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would like to introduce the prior testing of Dr. Roorda de Man into evidence. The Prosecutor has had a copy of this testing all along. It's really just a continuation. It's one set of psychological testing. Roorda de Man was able to do the intelligence part of the test, and then finally, with cooperation or with more response from Mr. Landzo, he has been able to do the projective testing. So as part of the psychological testing, I would like to introduce her initial testing results too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I'll have to use the witness' only copy right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, at some point prior to cross-examination, could I be provided with a copy of that?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes. I know this has been a part of the court's records for a long time, so I didn't make copies, but I'll certainly provide copies to the Defence counsel as soon as we have the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am not very clear. What's projective testing?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I'm going get the that because I wanted to explain his testing. So if you'll allow me to go on with my question, I'll get to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, when you went to see Mr. Landzo, you had not read any reports about him before and all you had was a brief ten-minute briefing by Dr. Lagazzi. What did you find when you met him? What was he like when you saw him? What was his personality?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Before the beginning of the testing or during the testing, I found a very well-suit person with a tie. And he seemed, to me, a person belonging to his Defence team, yes. I see him there, yes. He is the same as -- his clothes are the same or similar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he eager to visit with you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, he was eager, he was gentle. We shake our hands. He was concentrating on the task, but on one side -- on the other side he was rather impersonal. I didn't feel a lot of empathy from him to me and to the situation. He seemed to me a person keeping his control. And keeping everything around him very well controlled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you did this, performed this testing in June of this year, didn't you, and what dates were those?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: June 19th and 20th, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many hours do you think you spent performing this testing on Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I know -- eight hours, about eight hours during two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were performing this testing, it was a complicated process of Serbo Croat to Italian, Italian to -- you had two different interpreters?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, from Serbo Croat to Dutch and from Dutch to Italian. But, I succeed -- I succeeded in performing the test. And this complex situation didn't -- was a -- we succeeded in performing it. It didn't influence the results.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you explain to the Court what psychological testing is and what projective testing is?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, we can -- I say it briefly. Psychological testing is a complex field. It is a field developed by the first psychologist at the beginning of the century and the testing -- many things can be tested from intelligence to emotions, feelings and even mental condition. And the testing -- the field of the test divides into two main areas; the objective, the so-called objective tests, and the projective ones. For objective tests, measures some trait of personality, some -- some kind of ability or some kind of mental functioning, for example, intelligence and even some trait of personality we can measure it with the objective tests. And -- but objective test shows some problem because they're mainly in -- mainly constitute by questionnaires. That means you have some items, some question you have to answer. And then they're passed through the computer elaboration and at the end something mechanical comes out. And something very precise, very clear and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's the kind of testing that Dr. Roorda de Man performed, right?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Me, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, all the test that Roorda de Man succeed in performing were objective tests and she tried to evaluate the intelligence of Mr. Landzo. And she didn't succeed in doing the projective part of the tests. And we did it. I did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you tell Judge Jan what projective testing is?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, the patient is presented a neutral and not clear stimulus. And stimulus that's not related to the field that psychologists wants to know. And, for example, we can speak of the Rorschach test. The patient is presented upon the table upon which there is a big ink blot. And the patient is asked in -- is asked, what do you see upon the table? And it is sort of interpretation, like you could interpret the form of the clouds, for example. This is a game children play. And in seeing, in watching at tables and in seeing something, we say that the patient, the Rorschach say, that the patient projects something that he has inside him. That's his way of reacting to the stimulus and the -- and it can be seen by him outside. So projection means looking -- seeing outside what one person has inside, if I can speak so. And its projective tactics are very famous throughout the world. And especially the Rorschach was invented by Herman Rorschach in 1921. He studied psychology with Karl Gustav Jung. Since then lots of publications and books have appeared about it, for example. And I have explained the Rorschach while speaking of projective tactics, I have explain how is the Rorschach construct. And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second test that you performed was called the TAT. What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: It's slightly different from the Rorschach because the patient is not given not so -- not so-- a more detailed stimulus. The patient is presented with a picture in which there is some person, maybe some are photographs, some are pictures.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some are even blank, right?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, one, the 16th, yes, blank. And we say to the patient, "Look at it and imagine what can be, what could be there."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of the story you want to tell with that?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, imagine something, some picture upon it and say to me what story comes out from it, yes, what plot is there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for the Court's information, TAT stands for what? What are those initials?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Thematic Apperception Test because you look at the tables and when you look at it, you are asked to tell the story of that table and what do the main characters, the main persons in the table think and how is that situation, what happened and what will happen -- and what will happen in the future. So that is possible to see how, how a person constructs the plots. And some of that are very harsh, are very crude. For example, the 13th table is very crude. There is a man standing and the woman, a naked woman lying in her bed looking dead. And so, there has been a lot of difficulties of interpretation because people tend -- all people tend to see a situation of murder in it. For example, they think that, they say, oh, maybe this man, she was a former lover and he killed her, for example. So it has been a more difficult than the Rorschach to find a key to interpret it in a more formal way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A standard or a code?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, a code, because the Rorschach has a very complex coding, a formal one and depending on what, on what the patient has seen upon the table, I am speaking of the Rorschach. And there is a coding, a very complex coding -- a coding to locate what the patient has seen to determination of his response. For example, the shape or the colour or the shadow and so on and, according to the content what the patient has seen, for example, human response, animal response or object response or a nature or botanic or mask -- there is a lot of contents, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for the Court's information, the Rorschach test, the ink blocks, they start in black and white --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you progress different colours are added --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which also invoke different emotions?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, colours are connected to emotions and to activity. And we can see the way in which the patients manage their activity. And, for example, I don't want to anticipate anything, but Mr. Landzo was rather difficult in managing his activity, especially as concerns the red, the colour red that means, you know what red is, it's the colour of love, passion and blood, for example. And he had some problem in it. And we call shock. That means that the person is shocked by the colour and doesn't interpret it. And this is precisely what Mr. Landzo did, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the two projective tests that you did, they're widely accepted in the International Community of Psychology as valid tests, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, both. Even in the United States, Rorschach has been criticised because it's rather subjective interpretation. But I review, for example, this morning, Kaplan and Sadock, Synopsis of Psychiatry that my friend Lagazzi had and that you had. And I saw upon it that the Rorschach is considered one of the best ways, but must be interpreted by an expert psychologist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you, there is another test called the MMPI, would you tell the Court what that test is, and why did you not choose to use that test?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. If you remember the distinction I made before between protective and objective test is a personality questionnaire that is objective. And there are a lot of questions to which the patient has to answer true or false. And then all is passed through, through the computer and then comes out a lot of, a lot of scales come out of it and looking -- showing the different traits of the personality. But, in this case, we preferred not to -- not to performing not to do it because it is not culture free. There is a rather big cultural bias in it because it was -- it was studied and it was constructed in the United States, so it's full of reference to cultural themes more proper to the United States than to a Bosnian environment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, as you explained it to me, it may correctly project someone who is a white Anglo-Saxon Protestant American like me --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But as far as being cross-cultural, it does not take into consideration different cultures, so it cannot be accurate outside of the United States?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. And the Rorschach is rather culture free because it is based upon perception, so the way in which people see things, see ink blots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Doctor, your perception is also conditioned by your cultural background.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is, but not in the way it is -- the way -- not in the way the words are. The speech is much more. And, for example, from the point of view from intelligence, we have different testing and the most famous is WAIS. I think Dr. Roorda de Man performed some subtests belonging to it. And WAIS, Wexler Intelligence case is rather biased in the culture because it's mainly verbal. There is a non-verbal part, but it is just one half of the test. And there are other kind of testing that are more culture free, more free. If I remember, one of the PM, relevance, progressive -- PM 38, yes. PM 38 and PM 45, they are based more upon -- not upon phrases and words and discourse, but upon images. There are a lot of different flags showing some logical line, some logical progression. Then there is one flag lacking and you have to choose the appropriate response among eight or ten flags below. And on the lowest part of the sheet, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you, yesterday there was testimony about a term called malingering and I would like for you to say what that is, but also how the test that you performed are set to filter out and designed to bypass any malingering?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: There are two types of malingering. The one is the way one person can present himself. And, I don't know. Malingering could mean trying to appear differently from what one feels to be to the aim of manipulation, for example. And there is another kind of malingering that's not so conscious, but it's not malingering, but it's being -- having some, some tendency to play a part that's different. One is consciously seeking to present himself to the end of having a given result and one is not malingering, but is a tendency to, to wear a mask, I could say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the one is intentional and one is unintentional?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. Malingering in the narrow sense and the other is the tendency to play a part that's different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But these two tests that you did are designed to be able to detect real --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, because they are real. The patient doesn't know what to look for and looks at the table and sees what's upon it. So, it's impossible to -- oh, yes, it could be that someone came and say to the patient, oh, tomorrow the Rorschach will be performed upon you. You have to look just some kind of things, but we succeed in discovering it. But it's impossible, malingering in the more narrow sense I say it. And the second interpretation of the term that means playing a part, yes, it's possible to see it. Yes, it's possible to see the characteristic of the personality and especially the way in which colour response are treated by the patient. We have dramatised colours and false colours and we can see from it, we can detect the characteristic of a personality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you performed these tests, tell me how you apply them to a forensic kind of conclusion. How they are applied?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: They are very useful in forensic psychology or forensic psychiatry field because given -- because the patient cannot lie. And so in the forensic situation it happens that the patient comes and try to, to -- not to tell the truth and by such testing is a way of bypassing the problem because the patient doesn't know what the right answer could be in Rorschach or in TAT there is not the right answer. Every answer is accepted by the psychologist and coded according to the formal coding of that particular test. So it's possible to have an evaluation rather free from the malingering that you spoke of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you prepared a report after your testing on Mr. Landzo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that report is in front of you and before the judges and I am going to ask -- well, I'll wait until we're finished going through it. Can you tell me -- describe to the Court, the use of the coding in the TAT first and then in the Rorschach and then how you come up with a summary. Just go ahead and explain how you performed the testing and what this reflects?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. When I administer the test, I show the tables to the patient and the patient, you can see, for example, at page -- I take the English one. Yes, there. Page No. -- for example, page No. 1 you can see there is the text No. 1 means the first story told at the first TAT table and you see on the right side there is the coding, there is a formal one, a French one, coming from France and from the Sorbonne.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just to preface this, you gave an English legend that you wrote out this morning and just handed to me?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which explains that a G on this code which would be a W in English, which would mean whole, so that you can understand how we coded this?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: For example, if you take the Rorschach -- you can find it, there are three columns on the page, if you took every page, you can see on the left there is the response of the patient. For example, table No. 2, table No. 2, "You saw two things. I don't know, two animals, I can state two rabbits", for example. And then there is the inquiry because after the test has finished, we look again at the tables with the patient asking him where did you see that? How did you see it? Why did you see it? Show me and so on in order to understand, to better understanding of what -- why he saw the things he saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for clarity, the first one would be the patient's blank response?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second one would be after more interview with him, why he --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, for example, sometimes between brackets, I have put the words of the patient in the second column. The fist response, table No. 1, he seems -- he said blank, he seems like a person who is in a position ready to run. This is a reflected image of the same this thing. This is what it appears to me, a person. And then he explained, he is about to run away to the right, to the right direction, towards the right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: And that's my -- yes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said any time there is movement, that's an indication of intelligence or --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, of -- we could say intratension and that means -- it refers Karl Gustav Jung, division of personality, extroversion and introversion. And we say that's a sign of intelligence, of activity of that and of the mind, of the personality. But, for example, in this case, I have taken just the one in which he say he sees a blocked person. Ready to run, but blocked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But doesn't --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: He doesn't run, he tries to run, but stops, exerting his control upon it. And so that's the way in which he tries to exert his control upon things and is managing his, is controlling the whole situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these are -- these interpretations that you give these, these are fairly standardised throughout the international community?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That kind of interpretation?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Rather standardised, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to go on to getting to your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you go back to the TAT test, would you explain -- don't go into the testing itself, but explain to the Court your conclusions and why you came to that conclusion on the TAT test?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, if I could use the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Mainly two operating modalities of -- yes, of thinking of behaving, like two levels in the personality and the first we could say two levels, first level, the surface. And a deeper level, a more sincere one, the deepest. And apparently the patient functions rather well. He is intelligent, he is clever, he is -- in some way he succeeds in controlling the situation with intelligence. I would like to say that at the Rorschach, it can be see seen his intelligence as well. But his intelligence it showed in some way limited by an internal conflict, emotional conflict, a big one. So, apparently, it seems to function well from the intellectual point of view and that confirms Dr. Roorda de Man's conclusion that his intelligence is in some way above the average. So he functioning, but -- but at the TAT, there are a lot of clinical, formal signs of narcissism. That means that the story are plotted in a rather narcissistic way and there are not relationships between the persons, but mainly descriptions of how the persons feel, of their feelings and passions and what they feel from a -- even from a bodily point of view, warm, cold, the air, the atmosphere, all signs coded by -- that's the name of a French researcher. Like a sign of -- like a sign of narcissism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you too, when you speak of narcissism, are you applying this kind of conclusion to criteria in the DSM IV?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No. I'm speaking of narcissism from a psychodynamic point of view, and that means that the main concern of the subject, is aimed toward himself, so is mainly engaged with himself and he uses the others like a tool, like an instrument to have some, some advantage for himself, not considering the other from a caring, from a --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Empathetic?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, he was not empathetic, not during the examination. He was very kind, very friendly, but not empathetic from that point of view. And so we could say this level is well-functioning, but lacking concern for the others. I am trying to make -- to telling it in a not scientific, not technical way. That means narcissism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's what I asked Dr. Verde to treat me because I don't know what these terms mean so he is speaking like he is speaking to me.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Narcissism. Yes, another important characteristic of the TAT, we had some response, some answer for on clothing, on skin --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On outside.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: On the outside, yes. And that means that the patient is like he were wearing some clothes in order to appear, but not to be because the sense of identity comes from the lower child level, from the depth of the personality and he has not such kind of identity and he tries to appear and tries to stick to the other person in order to become --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To get -- to have an identity at all?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. And I say -- I saw him, for example, in this, I could call, a lawyer version of himself. And -- yes. And this kind of personality has been studied by psychiatry and psychoanalysts and that's what the famous psychoanalyst, Donald Winicott called false self. Because the true self is a self that has a surface, but is connected with the deeper level. The false self is something superficial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you're talking about the deeper level, did you find that it was empty, what did you find in the deeper level?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I might be getting you out of your order. You go ahead and explain your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, no. Yes, I am explaining upon the Rorschach now because the TAT is more near to the consciousness and it allows to us to go in-depth, but not in-depth as the Rorschach. The Rorschach shows there is a lot of mirror responses, that means narcissism. You know the story of Narcissi. At this level we found mainly is strange because the Rorschach he can function and he can manage his emotion. And, for example, the colours. But at the lowest level he cannot. And there was a particular response at the seven table of the Rorschach, the maternal one, and he saw a woman with something around her neck and something around the neck is the particular kind of response, it's how asthma shows himself at the Rorschach. I have to say asthma, in this condition, he had asthma in his childhood and that's the condition that affected him most in his early years. And asthma means a difficult relation with the mother. So we could speak of a child, you know, when the personality is well-structured, the child levels and the adult one are in good contact between -- there is a good contact between them and the child can work with the adult, with the parent inside and succeed and the child has the emotions and the adult control them and so on. But we have a sort of dividing line between one surface and the depth that's not so controlled. And at that level, there is the child, an ill, weak child with asthma, maybe with some problems with the mother, the figure of the mother, the -- there is a lot of stories of the TAT of pictures of the TAT that show one old woman that could be the mother and the patient spoke of the mothers in his stories in a very idealised way. Psychologists say, when you speak always well of a person, when you idealise her, there is a problem because every relationship has some problem. And the way a person has to deal with it and to manage it and to manage the conflict. If a person says there is no conflict, my mother is the best or the mother are at best in the TAT, there is some problem. So there is an over idealisation of the mother, that means that he had a lot of problems with his mother and that's a -- it is a problem to speak of it, of them. So, maybe -- we say that when we go to depth, we have to interpret something. We call this, in psychology, defence mechanism and idealisation is one of them. Idealisation on one side and splitting on the other. That means dividing the experience into two fields, one very good, very nice and one very bad. And when the -- when something -- when there is something, there is some difficulty at the childish level, the patient can become very aggressive. And that's the other finding of the test. And he is very scared, very anxious about his aggressiveness and he doesn't succeed very well in controlling it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on).

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Well, those are, of course, my last few questions. I am trying to get through these conclusions and how they apply to the questions that we have here and I think we're coming to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Doctor, before you proceed further, projective testing results, won't they vary with the passage of time because you get more experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Now, I am talking about projective testing results. Would they not vary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the same person, yes, they would vary very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In 1992, the result would be different from those in 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they should be. There is a speculation, but I could say the level of control of emotions by the patient, if in 1992 his condition were bad, control was lesser. So maybe that level, the functioning, well-functioning one were not so in control of the situation. And the other may be more prone to come out, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Particularly when you have traumatic experiences, particularly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, traumatic experiences can contribute to the worsening of the situation. And on the other side, good experiences can render it better, can render the performance better. For example, I saw the psychotherapist of the patient and we spoke for ten minutes in June and he say that the patient was behaving, was performing much better than a short time before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to clarify one thing, Dr. Verde, the conditions that you're describing from your testing of Mr. Landzo, they didn't just appear in 1992, this is a condition that began from early childhood?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah. It's a condition that is a personality. So the personality develops itself from the birth and from genetic factors and from -- mainly from -- research has shown that there are genetic factors that can influence the development of a personality, but the most important influence lies in the -- I could say emotional environment around the child. Winicott spoke of the good enough mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That scares me since I am here and my children are in Texas?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, but if you're concerned for them, that's okay. Yes, because capacity for concern and love is very important if the child feels that his mother cares for him and loves him and holds him. Winicott speaks of holding a person, the way in which the person is hold in the arms of the mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Verde, to summarise your conclusions from your testing, could you just tell us what conditions you found?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. I found a state of mind that can be called a marginal, borderline state in the sense of Karburg (Phon). That not mean borderline in the DMS 4 sense, but it show that the personality is functioning in a very complex and not well-suited way. And that means that we are in presence of a disorder, of a mental disorder. And that -- there are lot of problems in the patient, yes. It's called borderline -- borderline personality organisation. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from your testing, do you come up with labels of different conditions that he is suffering from or is that the next step with the psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I don't understand. Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am not even sure, myself, but when you come up with the fact that there is borderline condition --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that is fragile?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, fragile personality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this personality, do you come up with a label in your clinical testing or is that the next step that the psychiatrist --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, that's the psychiatrist. From the point of view of the personality, that's my diagnosis, borderline personality organisation, but I have not written it in my report. Let me see, complex personality which appears as apparently that he acted, but in reality it shows a rather heightened level of disturbance. That was the TAT. And the Rorschach, a complex personality who functions rather at the intellective than the effective level. He is experiencing notable problems with respect to human contacts and also secondary narcissism leading to a tendency to depend and idealise archaic, primitive and intensely loved object. These are compared by a notable aggressiveness which is base on the original depriving situation which is connected on the -- connected to an unsatisfied relationship with the figure of primary attachment, with the mother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these conclusions that you come up with, they are to find that there is a problem and they are explained in generic terms?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, a big one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would like to introduce his report into evidence at this point and I would like to introduce the one that has been corrected as far as terminology goes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may put it to him so that you can introduce it in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. I need the number of that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Defence document-D 51/4.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the markings that you have on this, explain your corrections as far as the interpretation goes?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because there was some technical problem in the translation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stand by the fact that this report that you prepared is accurate?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I move to introduce this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's admitted. The Prosecution has one, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they have one. Do you? I wasn't quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you how the authority figure in Mr. Landzo's life, whatever authority figure he has had, how that affects his behaviour?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: The authority figure, the main authority figure is the father in the development of personality. And maybe he had some problems with his father, but with his mother too. So we say that when things go well with the two parents, the personality development is okay. When things go badly, go badly with one of them, there must be the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stronger.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Stronger and ready to take and keep the child. And it's my opinion -- I have not written it in my report, but it's my opinion that both with the mother and the father, there have been a lot of problems from this point of view because you don't have so big a personality disorder if there is an one parent that loves the child and cares for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so with this big disorder that you're talking about, how does that affect his behaviour in dealing with other authority figures, not just his mother and father, but as he goes through?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: You know that we tend to live again in the same situation with important persons in our life. So, maybe he made displacement from the mother or from the father to the other person, trying to have from that person what he lacked, what he lacks in the internal relation or what he remembers about his child experience. So, our life is a continuous attempt at having what we didn't have from our past. So maybe he succeeded in finding him or not, but when he finds a parental object, that means -- that means a father or a mother or a person upon which to depend, he will behave in a very -- in a very -- in conformity, in a very similar way. And, for example, we have the lawyer here that I think may be connected to his relation with you or, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, based on your clinical evaluation and your clinical point of view, giving the predicate that Mr. Landzo suffered from a personality condition when he was young, can you say that he suffered from an abnormality of mind in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if he was suffering from an abnormality of mind in 1992, did this abnormality of mind influence his inability or ability to control his behaviour in the position of a guard at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah, of the behaviour and of the decisions about himself. We could use a metaphor. For example, the metaphor of the sight, of the visual field. If a person has a well-developed personality, he has a broad -- it's like having a broad visual field and can see things on the -- on both sides and even at the rear. But if a person has not a well -- a good development of his personality, its like having a more narrow visual field --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blinders?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Not blind, but maybe if normality is 200 degrees, if there is a personality disorder, it can be 60 degree. So you will see just these things and behave in conformity, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of the abnormality of his mind, would you say that he was in a state of diminished mental capacity?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Celebici in '92?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I pass the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will rise now and reassemble at noon when we will have cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are sill under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are there any cross-examination by the Defence? You might determine in what order you take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the order will be according to the indictment, but the Defence of Mr. Delalic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence of Mr. Mucic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess I am up. May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, please, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour Cross-examined by Mr. Moran

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, doctor.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I understand English is not your native language and sometimes I talk a little fast and sometimes I act like English is not my native language. So if I ask a question you don't understand, stop me.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I have the transcript on the screen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That may be helpful. My name is Tom Moran and I represent a man named Hazim Delic and I have a few questions that I want to ask you, based mainly on your direct examination and they're going to be pretty straightforward. I am not going to go into any kind of detail on your psychological testing, because, frankly, I don't understand it. But I do have a few quick questions. The first question, really, grows out of something in Dr. Roorda de Man's report. You're familiar with that report?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 8 of that report, she talks about Mr. Landzo's motor activities on the Perdue Peg Board?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, it's the second paragraph from the top in the English version. I am happy to let you borrow my copy so you can find it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let's start with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is a Perdue Peg Board, pray tell?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: That's not my report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know it's Dr. Roorda de Man's report, but, yes, she said you were familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is a Perdue Peg Board and what does it measure?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I don't see in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The paragraph that has the star next to it, the second paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Perdue Peg Board, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, that's a good answer.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: It's probably a test to measure the motor capacity, the motor activity that belongs to the neuro-psychological field and it was called neuro-psychological field for people working with, for example, motor impairment, for example, Vietnam Veterans, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, in various reports, including Dr. Lagazzi's --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- There recounts that Mr. Landzo claimed that he had head injuries as a child?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, typically, where I come from, a neuro-psychologist would perform testing to see if there is organic brain damage based on that. Is that the kind of thing we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah, for example. But this motor, this motor in the Perdue Peg Board may need some motor capacity, so the capacity to take things in and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, organic brain damage can cause -- it can be minor, caused by head injuries and it can cause people to behave in inappropriate ways; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: It can, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Violent?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never -- you don't do that kind of testing, do you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, that requires postdoctoral training?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, it's a different kind of testing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: It's not a broad, as broad as the test I did. That is narrow. And I can see -- I would like to explain to you, I could see the presence of brain damage in the Rorschach. It could be seen easily, rather easily, even when it's not manifold, even if not -- even little minimal signs of brain damage can be seen at the Rorschach, rather easier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Rather easily, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Doctor, I promise you that your English is much better than my Italian. Judge Jan is smiling because that's a standing joke. I usually say someone's English is much better than my Bosnian. And It's been my experience that professionals, especially neuro-psychologists will tell me that this kind of brain damage can cause, or organic brain damage in general, can, among other things, cause people to behave violently, often times. For instance, they will testify in my country in murder trials saying that this person is not necessarily responsible for what he did because of the organic brain damage?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Not only neuro-psychologist, but even psychologists and psychiatrists, because psychologists and psychiatrists make a broad evaluation of the personality. So it is possible to see such damage. And, for example, if you want to ask me if I saw that in Mr. Landzo, I will answer to you that I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. Secondly, in, again, Dr. Roorda de Man's report, and her testimony was that she didn't accede in doing the projective part of the testing because he was not interested and could not relate to anything?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you examined Dr. Lagazzi's report from May the 15th -- or, excuse me, November the 15th, 1996?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing in there -- and in the English version, it's page 26 of the report, if you have it in front of you.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. That, essentially, he presented that he had an inability to concentrate -- the exact quote is, "The ability to concentrate was objectively limited, without, however, manifesting grossly pathological features." And in the next paragraph, Dr. Lagazzi says, "His logical faculties were shown to be reasonably adequate in the first three interviews, while at the last one they appeared to be practically nil."

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those two reports are consistent with each other, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the report Dr. Lagazzi did just a couple of weeks ago?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe it's dated the 3rd of July?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the portions -- and if you like, I can go find them for you.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah, it would be better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where Dr. Lagazzi reports that Mr. Landzo, "On some occasions, as he now admits, he simulated disorders of awareness and orientation, which were not compatible with the clinical reality of the case?"

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am just going to object to this line of questioning. Dr. Lagazzi will be testifying tomorrow. He is the best one to testify for this report. And Dr. Verde said he only read it, you know, briefly, after he tested Mr. Landzo, so it really has no relevance to his results in this case. And I think the best evidence would be for him to ask Dr. Lagazzi about these reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He is merely asking him whether he has read it. And then he may ask whatever questions he will want to. I don't see how it's not relevant. If he is also a specialist and he is giving evidence in this case, these are areas in which they have all cooperated and will be saying what they knew about the subjects. So, I don't see how it is not relevant. It's quite relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I just want to explain, too, that he didn't read those reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has asked him and he said he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I am going to ask a question because Dr. Lagazzi, who is sitting out in the audience, is going to hear the answer, it may be a delicate question. You have worked with Dr. Lagazzi for quite a while, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I have been working with him for, I think, 15 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're friends?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know him real well? You know him well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Fifteen years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he is a good psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he is not likely to be fooled by someone who is --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, not at all. He has a lot of clinical and forensic experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure. And so, if back in November of 1996, Dr. Lagazzi reported that these logical faculties were practically nil in the last interview and then in July of 1998 he says, wait a second, the patient admitted to me that -- what's the exact phrase? Patient admitted, essentially, that he was feigning this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why don't you give the consideration of what Lagazzi says when he comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I was going to ask the witness was, if it would be unusual for Dr. Lagazzi to be fooled by somebody like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You ask him, because he is coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And malingering --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and your tests are objective tests designed to leave out malingering, but people have malingered and fooled very good mental health professionals, haven't they?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't think that this is the case because the quality of the projective testing renders it impossible to fool the psychologist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Even in view of the patient's admission that he simulated disorders of awareness and orientation?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, because I spoke to Mrs. McMurrey about two kinds of malingering. The first one is consciously trying to convince, to persuade the other person. And the second -- and that's the -- and that's the thing that people cannot do with this kind of testing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, DSM IV, you're familiar with DSM IV?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It warns practitioners about malingering, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object. First of all, this psychologist has said he does not use the DSM IV in his testing. He did not rely on the DSM IV. So his question about DSM IV to this clinical psychologist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why don't you listen to his answer? He asked him whether he is familiar with the DSM IV. He said yes. That was his answer right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: It's irrelevant because he didn't use DSM IV in his testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You're not even an expert, what business have you answering for him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The DSM IV says that in some situation there is a danger of simulation, like every textbook of psychiatry, for example, I have here Kaplan and Sadock. And in the forensic section at the end of the book, it tells the same thing. So it's for that reason that we do test. That is the field in which psychological testing is widespread throughout the world because these kind of testing renders to the person very difficult, the simulation, the malingering, the consciously attempt at persuading the others about something not true about themselves, about the personality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one of the times when DSM IV tells you to watch out, especially for malingering, is in a medical/legal situation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is that? What is a medical/legal situation, doctor?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: The medical/legal situation is the situation which a person has to be evaluated, like this situation, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, for instance, if a person, one of my clients --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- Arthur Brown Jr., a man used to be one of my clients, did not want to go to death row, he might try to feign mental illness?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: It depends.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this calls for speculation. He is certainly not familiar with an American death row inmate right now and he has not said that he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know why you are allowing me to intervene every time. I think you're becoming a bit awkward. Let him answer the question, it's a simple thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, maybe. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: (Microphone not on).

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour he is currently a resident of death row. But there were four dead bodies to explain away in a robbery, so it was a little tough. Hopefully he'll get a new trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think it's essentially intended deceive the other --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I don't interrupt judges, judges interrupt me. I'm sorry, Judge, go on ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, in one particular diagnosis in the DSM IV, the diagnosis for antisocial personality disorder, that practitioners are especially warned to watch for lies and malingering because people who have antisocial personality disorder tend to be good liars; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, some of them are very personable people?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They're personable? They're nice folks, you enjoy being around them, they've got a nice personality?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yea. But you know, the personality disorder in the DSM -- the psychiatrists call it co-mobility, you can have many diagnosis of the same persons together. If I remember well, 60 per cent of the patient diagnose it with one personality disorder at the DSM III and IV had at least another diagnosis in the same section, another personality disorder.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wouldn't be at all uncommon, for instance, to have access to his personality disorders, to have two or three different diagnosis in that same axis, would it? With the first one listed being the primary diagnosis and then becoming --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Maybe, I didn't do such a diagnosis. I did psychological one and so I am, I am not familiar with that kind of reasoning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, basically what your job was, was to do psychological testing --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to provide to Dr. Lagazzi, to aid him in his diagnosis? Is that a fair assessment of what your job was?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I did my job and then I gave him -- I gave it to the Defence attorney and then she gave it to Lagazzi yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basically you were to provide data for Dr. Lagazzi?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, as I said, I didn't speak with about the case to Lagazzi, except for a few phrases, about ten minutes, about Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to your testing?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to testing?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've talked to him about it since the testing? I mean, you had dinner with him for crying out loud.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: After doing my report, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Fine, thank you very much, Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry. Cross-examined by Mr. Cowles:

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Cross-examined by Mr. Cowles:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Verde. My name is Jim Cowles, I represent the Prosecutor in this matter.
