utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Dr. Verde, that many criminals have personality disorders?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah, it can be. Yes, it's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Also non-criminals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, personality disorders, they -- people that have personality disorders are more prone to act than the other people, especially the second cluster of DSM IV that's the so-called dramatic cluster, borderline and antisocial and narcissistic, they are prone to act, to have -- to have outbursts of rage and to -- what we call acting out in psychology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is what you found in Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Not at all. I found a rather maintained capacity to control himself and the situation. But, in some fields, he lacks the reality test. That means he doesn't evaluate well his current situation and reality. Let me make an example. For example, his behaviours towards the guards in the UN detention unit during the test, he behaved with the guards like he were their boss, for example. He said, do that or don't do that and so on. That was, sort of reality test that lacked in that particular field, the field of authority. So -- and I explain it in a psychological way by calling that defence mechanism, the defence mechanism of identification with the aggressor, for example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that fits your definition, then, that you found narcissism and a capacity in Mr. Landzo to use other people as objects of exploitation?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this was an example.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, at the end of your testimony, your direct examination with Ms. McMurrey, you gave several opinions concerning Mr. Landzo's -- your opinion of Mr. Landzo's mental condition in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's nowhere addressed or mentioned in your report, is it?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, because my report refers to the situation, to his psychological condition, to his present psychological condition, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you testified that not being an MD, you're not a doctor, your purpose as a psychologist to give test results to a psychiatrist to make a medical diagnosis; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not presuming to make a medical diagnosis of Mr. Landzo's condition in 1992, are you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: It's a complex field. In Italy we had a lot of problems. I am a member of the Chamber of Psychologists in my town and that's a question. We can do psychological diagnosis. We can do it, but we have a sort of a category conflict with the field, yes. But we do. In some way we do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you answered Ms. McMurrey concerning her last questions, you specifically stated that your opinion of Mr. Landzo's mental condition in 1992 is pure speculation; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's not what he said in the record. He never mentioned the word speculation. I don't know where the prosecutor is coming up with misstating the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am looking at the transcript from LiveNote right now, where the witness specifically uses the word that his opinion is speculation as to Mr. Landzo's condition in 1992. I can reference the page and line number from LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, the witness is here and can he confirm exactly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Basing, myself, on what I have seen, I can, in a scientific way, try to give an explanation of how he was, for example, six years ago. And I have answered to Mrs. McMurrey that his condition is a rather structural, stable one. It's not a passing condition. It's a condition of personality and has to be traced backwards until his childhood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that his personality hasn't changed since childhood?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: It hasn't changed so much because there is a splitting, a division, a splitting in his personality. So, the lower, the basic part is not much changed in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But my question is, you used the term "speculation," aren't you speculating as to his condition in 1992?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: If speculation means to go from what I see to what I didn't see, because I was not there, it's speculation. But I can say a scientific conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, you don't know any of the facts of the case, do you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't know what Mr. Landzo is alleged to have done over a course of time in 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I have heard that he is accused of some crime, yes, some homicide, murder, yes. I have heard it, but not more, not details. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How he committed?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did not discuss with Mr. Landzo any facts about what, or accusations, about what --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, that's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination? Before then, I should give you an opportunity to reply to that. Professor, one of your conclusions is that he has an abnormality of mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: One of your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What are the manifestations of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The manifestation in behaviour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, from what you have known about him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, the proneness to acting out, to aggressiveness. And, for example, the taking the others' clothes and being, being -- you know, we speak of identification. Identification means that you have a father inside and you want to be like him in order to be an adult, for example. And he has not such a capacity, but he tends to put on, to wear the clothes of the others. It's rather like an animal, a chameleon. I don't know if you understand me. I don't know the English word, but it should be minuses, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Metamorphosis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, change colour according to the environment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Chameleon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are those the considerations that you took for determining that he had abnormality of mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's based upon the results of the testing. And I have seen this capacity to put the others close in my testing. And I have seen the two levels, not as a complex mind, but is, rather, a split mind from my testing, yes. It's a formal -- it's a formal coding of the answer of the patient to the test, yes. And it's widely recognised throughout the world that this kind of psychological tools, yes. The Rorschach, I think is the most famous test, projective test in the world. Every people know, or Rorschach, ink blot, yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How did you relate that to his behaviour during the period he was a guard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe he could, trying to be a perfect guard, in order to, in order to be praised and appreciated by his boss, for example. Because he is -- I didn't mention the fact today that he has a deep lack of self-esteem. And in order to have -- to maintain his self-esteem, he has to depend upon the, upon the esteem of another person. So, I don't -- I don't have self-esteem, so I need to have your self-esteem to not to be depressed. And when he lacks the self-esteem, the esteem of the other, he will be depressed and he will be feel feelings of emptiness and void. And all these conclusions, I draw them from my testing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, you may proceed. Re-examined by Ms. McMurrey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to go back to Dr. Lagazzi's report that Mr. Moran has asked you about.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know, since you only read it for a short period of time, if you can remember, in that report, did Dr. Lagazzi say that, of course, he seemed to not be responding to any stimuli, but Dr. Lagazzi added in that --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Even Dr. Roorda de Man says that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Dr. Lagazzi in November of '96 said, I believe that he is manipulating me at that moment. He was able to recognise that, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's why he didn't continue in that evaluation at that time? I take that back, you can't answer that question, I'm sorry. Now, Mr. Cowles asked you, many criminals have personality disorders. What we're talking about here is not a merely a personality disorder, it's an extreme pervasive disorder that has gone all throughout the life of Mr. Landzo; would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think the key word that you were looking for is pervasive, which means that it covers every facet of his life?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not just 1992?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, no, since he was a child. He had asthma and a big suffering, yes. Especially when it's severe, like I think in this case, Roorda de Man speaks about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I mean, are you seriously suggesting that asthma is another contributing factor to this type of behaviour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe asthma is caused by -- I don't know, because it's considered a psychosomatic disorder, asthma. And the difficulty to breathe has to do with the relation with the mother. And the -- the child psychiatry has done a lot of research about psychosomatic illnesses and maybe a difficult relation with the mother causes asthma and other difficulties, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is he still asthmatic now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: We have a Dutch doctor coming to address that later on this afternoon who evaluated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I know a very good many people who are asthmatic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if you're asthmatic, it does not mean that you are a delinquent.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I clear this up? He is not saying that everybody who suffers from asthma has a personality disorder. And would you explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Asthma is not connected to personality disorder, but it is a condition of intense suffering. And the personality disorder can -- one can have a personality disorder even without asthma, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And people can be normal with asthma, without having a personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what happens here, asthma was an aggravating factor with someone who started out with a personality disorder?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, it can be, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to many criminals who have personality disorders, we're talking about -- you're evaluation of Mr. Landzo is not based on whether criminals have it, it's based on the individual person because you're not applying this to any criminal conclusion or legal conclusion?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the, the word that Mr. Cowles kept saying was, your speculation about 1992, did you really mean to say projection back?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, maybe, because I -- I didn't do psychological interview to Mr. Landzo. I did speak some minutes before the testing. And I didn't ask him how he was in 1992, like I think all the psychiatrists or expert have made. But I limit myself to the passing of the -- of the testing. So I didn't ask him how -- I didn't recollect an (inaudible).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand that last word.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: The latent term is (inaudible).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that like amnesia?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am trying to --

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, no, no, when you ask the patient to say to you how he was and what kind of illness he had and when -- what type -- and when you were born, for example, the life was nice, and then you have everything was normal and what kind of disorders of illness you had and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that kind of study is done by the psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, that's a physician, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not through psychological testing?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, even by the psychologist. For example, Roorda de Man did, but I had that, I had the specific task of doing the testing, so I did just that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the opinions that you came up with earlier, as far as abnormality of the mind, that is based strictly on your clinical diagnosis of international accepted testing procedures, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, we met this morning at eight o'clock?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To decide what we're going to talk about today --

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, I do object to this, this is not proper re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's not re-examination, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well then, leave it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: This is re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: On whose cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: On Mr. Cowles' cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What was his question that is ambiguous?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He tried to say that he didn't base his opinions on psychological, clinical testing. And what I am trying to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He answered that, that he projected from conclusions he had, he now came to the assumption that it could be -- no, that's what the witness himself said.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Mr. Cowles started off his cross about the conclusions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it did not arise out of it. He answered your questions and you don't have to go further.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The conclusion that I asked you to come up with dealt with mental capacity in 1992. I never asked you to determine mental responsibility, which is a legal conclusion, did I?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you for being here, Dr. Verde.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We're very grateful for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before he leaves, if can I get my report back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your book?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, my report from -- whatever her name is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Roorda de Man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you are discharged. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's have your next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Defence calls Elmir Hadzajlic. Your Honour, I want to bring to the Court's attention, I am not sure that the victim and witnesses has him here right this minute. I think that they had projected that he would come after lunch. But he is one of the witnesses who was on the list today -- I mean, right now. He may be here at 2.30 instead of right now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness is not available.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Then I ask the Court if we just stop a few minutes early and come back with that witness after lunch?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So you're expecting him after lunch?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: He is at the Bel Air Hotel. We can get him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We'll break for lunch and come back after lunch at 2.30. 21 22 23 24 25 --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mrs. McMurrey, if you're ready. Swear the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Elmir Hadzajlic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: You just read that out in open court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seat, please. Cross-examined by Ms. McMurrey

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you introduce yourself to the Court, please, what is your name?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: My name is Elmir Miro Hadzajlic, from Konjic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzajlic, are you having difficulty keeping the headset on your head because you don't have any hair?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, it's better? Okay. You met yesterday with me and with Ms. McHenry, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I just want to explain to you, you've never testified in court before, have you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you a little nervous about being here today?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Of course I am, a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, I think if you could move a little closer to the microphone, or pull the microphone closer to you, we might be able to hear you a little better.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Is that better?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Still closer, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: The interpreters say a little closer. And I want to explain to you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's going to be interpreted and I am going to ask you a question, and it's going to be a little while before you can answer me because you listen to the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and I first met in Konjic, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you tell the Court what your business is in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I am a private entrepreneur. I deal in trade and catering. I have a couple of private facilities in town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say catering, you have one of the best restaurants in town, don't you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: You were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what I said. You were in the same kind of businesses before the war started in Konjic, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the war started -- after the war started, you left Konjic and went to Split and travelled as a refugee, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, when you left, you had a large inventory of food and goods and everything and you donated those to the defence cause, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I donated most of those goods for the defence cause.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did you know, or did you know a young man named Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. I can't recognise him now, only just managed to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, now that you brought him up, how does he look different today than he did in 1991 and '92 when you knew him?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: When I knew him, he was a real child. And now, as far as I can see, he is a grown man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, you said you knew him in 1991 and '92, how did you come to know Esad Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: He came to see me. He came to my company with a colleague of his who used the work for me, Zdravko Stipatic, whom we called Tipa (Phon). I needed some assistance. I had some work to be done, I think a truck with goods had arrived, and he brought him along and that is when he started working for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say he worked for you, he worked for you mainly for food and items to take to his family and you guaranteed that he would have pocket money; is that kind of what your agreement was?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, we could call it an agreement of that kind because the times were quite unusual then. Salaries were paid in goods. Very often only a smaller share in money. But I gave him whatever he asked for. And he asked for very little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he worked for you, did he come to work for you as a like a guard and a general helper in your warehouse area?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I haven't objected in preliminary, but I would ask that counsel not lead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of duties did he perform, Mr. Hadzajlic?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: He did everything, loading, unloading, guarding goods, security of the goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you describe for the Court what kind of worker Esad Landzo was?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: As a worker, he was extremely diligent, honest and hard-working, honest, obedient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, would you say that if you had an opportunity to hire 20 Esad Landzo's, would you do that?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: It would be difficult to find others like him, but I would, indeed, hire them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he like the perfect worker for you, the perfect employee?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object to leading again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has already answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: His last answer was more than any you could ask for again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Oh, I could ask for more, Your Honour, but I won't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how old was Esad Landzo at the time he worked for you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I think he was 17 or 18. Believe me, I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And when was it about that he came to work for you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: This was in the middle of 1991, in the first half of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he worked for you until what period of time?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I think it was until the 1st of June, 1992. I think it was the 1st of June in '92. I can't recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can't be sure about those dates; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I would like for you -- was Esad Landzo the kind of boy who looked up to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Naturally, he was a small boy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, but that's the evidence I need to get for the Court, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Any boy would look up to his employer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not anything unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, it's not anything unusual, except we're going further with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, he would do almost anything to please you, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I am going to object again to the leading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would he do anything, almost anything to please you?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I still object to the leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What you want is what he was to him as a worker.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he was more than a worker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask him that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Landzo more than a worker for you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, did you even use him to work for you at your house?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of things would Mr. Landzo do for you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: At home he would do cleaning, washing, fixing the fire for a barbecue, anything that needed to be done, he would do it. And also, he would watch over the house in my absence. And he could use everything he needed in the house. It was at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you have a lot of trust in Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have keys to your facilities, to your shops?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: He slept in the shop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, in fact, I would like to ask you to tell the Court about the experience you had with Mr. Landzo at your girlfriend's birthday party.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: This was on the 26th of May, 1992, my girlfriend, future wife, was celebrating her birthday. We were celebrating at her place and we ran short of wine. I called him up, he was in my house, and I called him to bring two crates of wine. As soon as I hung up, the shelling of the town started. And I think 30 to 40 shells fell around the house of my wife. These shells were of considerable destructive power. And we hid in the cellar. While the shelling continued, somebody started banging on door. None of us dared go out. I went out and saw Esad Landzo who had brought us the wine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you tell another -- would you explain to the Court an incident where you went to the front-line to defend Konjic against the Serb attack?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: There was a point in time when all people in town who had arms were called upon to gather closer the front and they came to my restaurant. Esad had an uniform and this Zdravko Stipatic also had an uniform. I saw the two of them and we had an automatic rifle. However, I saw that Zdravko, who was of heavier build and stronger than Esad, was a bit scared, which was only natural, all of us were scared. I took a uniform from Tipa, this is Zdravko Stipatic, and the automatic rifle and I left the two of them in the restaurant and I went to the first line closest to the front. And there were about 50 of us volunteers who had gathered there and we were told that strong Chetnik forces were launching an attack against the town from the direction of Borci. We waited there for an hour to go to the actual front-line, we waited for orders to that effect. In the meantime, both Tipa, and Esad Landzo came unarmed to go with me to the front-line to fight the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they showed up at the front-line without any weapons following you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you consider Mr. Landzo brave?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I consider him to be extremely brave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Landzo never told you anything about any physical problems he had, did he?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything about it, I don't recall. Yes, he had a hand that was -- or, rather, his fingers was slightly bent, but this was hardly noticeable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, as far as you know, he worked and did everything that you requested, including the loading and unloading trucks?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court why you think he didn't tell you about his physical problems?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he knows the man very well and he can form an opinion as to why he would not have told him about his problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I am allowed to ask him, his opinion as the why Mr. Landzo did some other things, then I won't object.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I believe she has a right to ask that question, if he knows, and if he has an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The answer did not tell him of his handicap.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's very important right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, ask him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you think Mr. Landzo didn't tell you about his handicaps?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I believe that he feared that he might be fired by me. That he wouldn't be able to carry out the tasks I gave him to do because, for instance, we didn't have a forklift, everything had to be unloaded by hand, up to 20 tons of good sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think he may have thought you might have thought less of him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Objection. She asked the question, and the witness answered and now she's leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Okay, I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When June of '92 came, you tried to persuade Mr. Landzo to stay with you, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he left, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. I wanted to persuade him to stay because he was still a child. I wanted to persuade him not to go anywhere so as to save his life. Because, after all, I was a bit older and more mature and I could protect him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one more question. You have a nickname, don't you that everybody knows you by.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: My name is Elmir Miro, they call me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Miro.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: I am going to pass the witness now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have two and if I can do it from here, it would be a lot quicker, with court's permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you have any questions, you ask. Cross-examined by Mr. Moran

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you said Mr. Landzo worked for you continually from the first half of 1991 through about the first of June, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, you may ask questions. Cross-examined by Ms. McHenry

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, when Mr. Landzo worked for you from the first half of 1991 to the middle of 1992, how much did he work for you? I mean, everyday? Most days? Once a week or once a month? Can you give us an idea about that?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: As far as I know, he worked everyday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He was a regular employee, that's what he means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't remember any time when he was gone for three weeks or more, do you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Landzo worked with a close friend of his, didn't he? He and a close friend of his, Mr. Landzo both worked for you, correct?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: Yes. Stipatic Zdravko called Tipa.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you testified about Mr. Landzo bringing you several crates of wine. Among the other things that Mr. Landzo did was unload items, including TV sets and canned goods; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: He did everything from loading, unloading to cleaning, security, guarding the goods and everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And among the things that he did was unload items, such as TV sets, correct?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: There were all kinds of goods, TV sets, video recorders, refrigerators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Has TV sets any particular significance? He was unloading and unloading.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am just trying to get to his physical capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir you already talked about that you didn't notice any difficulties in carrying out his duties with his hand. You didn't notice any problem with his breathing either, did you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I didn't notice that he had problems with his hands while working, but one could see that his hand wasn't quite normal. I think it was something like that, but he could conceal that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you didn't notice any problems with Mr. Landzo's breathing, did you?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I didn't really watch him while he was unloading, nor did I supervise him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But to the extent that you observed him during this time he worked for you, you never noticed any problem with his breathing, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How many times have you asked this one question? He said he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you trusted Mr. Landzo. Is it therefore correct that you didn't notice any mental problems with Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: I didn't notice any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, and is it also correct that when the war started, Mr. Landzo ignored your advice and did what he wanted to do and joined the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Alfredo Verde
utterances.text: If he had listened to my advice, he would have stayed with me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: One question, Your Honour Re-examined by Ms. McMurrey:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Miro, what your testimony was earlier, you didn't remember the exact dates that Mr. Landzo came to work for you, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He already said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Several times. Several times, almost a year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure of the dates. Let me, let me underline that. I am not sure of the dates. Which dates they were, when he started working exactly and when he exactly left I cannot assert with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Miro, for being here. Thank you. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony. You were very helpful and kind. Thank you. You are discharged now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour and I wanted to ask the Court's permission, the next two witnesses are the Dutch doctors who are coming to testify and they're in Ms. Boler's province right now. And we have a new attorney joining us that I would like to have permission to sit in the Court while I go visit with some other witnesses that are here. So if you'll excuse me from the Court and allow Mr. Calvin Sanders to join Ms. Boler while she examines the next two witnesses. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the Court's permission, I would like to be excuse and Mr. Cowles will be handling the next two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Who is now leading your witness? Because we have not seen any of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be doctor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You shall bring him in. (Witness entered)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is the witness testifying in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We discussed this earlier. There was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel switch on the microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did make arrangements for a Dutch interpreter, but he told me just a few minutes ago that he is comfortable testifying in English. Is that your preference? There is a Dutch interpreter directly bind you. What would be your preference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The witness speaks for himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, introducing your new counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: You want me to do that now before he is sworn?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to introduce to you, Mr. Calvin Sanders. Mr. Sanders is a lawyer from New York City and been practising about 14 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SANDERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: And just about a week ago had an opportunity to meet Mr. Sanders, and since we needed a legal assistant, we invited him to join our team. He was here in The Hague already taking a course in international criminal law. He is happy the join us and we're happy to have him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Welcome to the Landzo team and I hope you'll be very helpful to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SANDERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seats, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I begin --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Sorry. Before we begin, may I just ask the usher if he will give the witness a copy of his report and his curriculum vitae. And I also have copies for everybody else. It's of the report.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Document D 54/4. Examined by Ms. Boler:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Haeseker.

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And thank you for coming today. Would you please begin by stating your name for the Court.

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Do I have to stand?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: My name is Barry Haeseker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how are you employed, Dr. Haeseker?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: I am presently employed by the main hospital of the Hague, Leyenburg Hospital. And I am also working in the hospital for sick children and the rehabilitation, plastic surgeon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what percentage of your practice is devoted to plastic surgery, to hand surgery?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, that's about 40 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what types of things do you do in your practice as a plastic surgeon for hands?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: On hands, we do in congenital hand defects, all kind of injury to hands, burns to hands and disease of the hands, like the (inaudible) rheumatoid disease, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a little bit about your educational background. Can you tell the Court what your educational background is?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, I was born in Amerongen, the centre of this country. And I was educated in Harlem, in Amsterdam. And there I went to secondary school. Afterwards, I went to the medical school in Amsterdam, until 1970. And then I went to the tropics, to Malawi for three years as a district medical officer. Afterwards, I came back, did my general training in general surgery and plastic surgery. First in Delft and then later in Wales, in Chepstow for another year. And then the main education in plastic surgery was for three years in Rotterdam.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long have you been practising at the Leyenburg Hospital where you are now?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Since 1982.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And let me draw your attention back to, I guess, a couple of months ago at this time. Did I contact you at some point and ask you if you would be available to be a witness in this capacity before the tribunal?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, as a part of that, did you go to the UN Detention centre and have a visit with Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you then write a report about the findings after having that visit with Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote a short report.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wrote it in Dutch actually, correct?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Dutch, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I have shown you a copy of the translation?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that translation of your report an accurate report of what you stated?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, I just saw -- there are a few misprints that I saw, but not too much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it anything that substantially changes your report?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: No, not substantial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll give you an opportunity to point those things out. And, Your Honours, at this time, I would like to introduce the report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution seen it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Yes, the prosecution has seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: If it's the one page report that's very short, we do have that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let's hear the correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The correction -- well, I just saw today, I saw, for example, some misprints, like treatment I saw over there. So that was not exactly what I had said. I have the original here, that is the Dutch one. Overall, I think the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to go through the report with him and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What we expect to be admitted is the corrected version. The version which the expert has corrected has his report, not the one which has errors, which he complains about.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we discussed this report earlier today and, perhaps, I could have him do what Dr. Verde did a little while ago is to just in his handwriting tell me the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We'll follow his reading of the report and we'll see where the correction lies and we'll correct it. And then he'll admit it, so then we'll define our report and that is the report he is submitting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: We'll are to admit it into evidence after we've gone through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: That will be fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you --

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Oh, yeah, contractions was there, it was contractors, but that is what I saw, and that's not exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: We'll go through this report and I'll give you an opportunity to correct anything that you see. I believe the one you're talking about now is about two-thirds of the way down, where the first line says, "contractors," correct?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it should say contractions?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Contractions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made this report based on a discussion that you had with Mr. Landzo at the UN Detention Centre, correct?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the report you mentioned how the accident occurred and how he actually sustained the hand injury. Can you tell the Court what you learned about the hand injury?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, he told me that he had a quarrel with his father in 1991 and that he had a knife in his hand and a clenched fist and that he hit the wall, he stabbed the wall with it. Then he got some cuts in Finger 2, 3, 4 and 5 on the right hand. And in the 2nd and 3rd hand was very superficial, skin only. And in 4 and 5 he had a damage of the flexortendons. And in the 5th also, probably of the -- of the nerve, on the radial side. And those two, the fingers, 4 and 5, were treated in a kind of a Kleinert way in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe what the Kleinert technique is?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, it's kind of a direct operation in the area what we call "No Man's Land" that is within the flexortendon sheaf. And there you have to stitch it up properly and do a very good after treatment with a rubber bandage through the nail. And you fix that through the wrist, so you can practice without really involving the tension on the knot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of the treatment that he did receive in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: That is a specialised -- it is a specialised type of treatment and they don't call it "No Man's Land" for nothing. It is someone's land. It is for plastic hand surgeons who are doing that often. If you don't do that very often and give not a good after treatment, then it all can become fixed. It will heal the tendons, but it will not work very properly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your understanding of the after treatment that he received there?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, what I do understand, it was not a very good after treatment due to conditions of the country in that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If he had been treated by you, for example, if you had been the initial treating physician, what, perhaps, might have been different with the results of that injury?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, you're never sure, of course. I haven't seen the initial wound so I have to guess a little bit. But, if it was a clear cut, damage of the 4th and the 5th finger, then of the 4th finger prognosis is normally good and the 5th finger is a difficult finger because everything is small over there and that could be less better than the 4th, but the 4th should be all right to function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also discussed some possibilities for treatment in the future and how that might affect it. Could you just briefly tell the Court what might be available?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, there is also a little bit of pain in the 5th finger due to neuromyal formation. I just forgot to mention that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what neuroma is?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Neuroma is a painful little tumour due to damage or anything else, what can cause a lot of pain by touch and that's normally due to damage on the nerve. And I don't know exactly if the nerve was repaired in Yugoslavia because they needed a microscope.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to feel that neuroma when you did the physical examination?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yes, you can feel it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you to say that it was on the 5th digit only, or is there a neuroma in both the 4th and the 5th digit?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: No, it was a local pain by pressure in the 5th finger, not in the 4th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a type of amputation, can you explain --

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: When you want to do something to give a better function of the hand, yeah. The 4th finger, I think you can still do something about it by doing a secondary repair of the tendons. The 5th finger, it has a bad prognosis and -- well, you can amputate it, it's very drastic, of course. You can do a partial amputation. You can also make a joint stiff, an arthrodesis as we call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the advantage of doing an amputation to that 5th digit?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, if it is just in the way, you can sometimes better get it off and you feel a bit better. But it's very drastic, you don't do it normally, but it's a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go on. If you'll follow me in your report, you'll see a Capital D and a Capital R. And then can you explain what the Capital D is?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: D is diagnosis and R is treatment. And what the diagnosis was flexortendon damage to 4th and the 5th finger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain what flexortendon damage is, if it's anything other than what that you've already discussed?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: No, I think I discussed already. But there are two tendons in each finger with the exception of the thumb. And we call it profundus et superficialis. That's also a misprint, it should read superficialis with an F. And so means a superficial tendon and a deep tendon. And they were both cut. And that is the diagnosis: They were cut at that time. There's probably also vascular damage due to an artery in the finger and nerve damage in Digit 5. And the arm means treatment. Well, the flexortendons has been stitched, but, well, we're not very sure that there is any after treatment, probably not a good after treatment and follow up. And there is a nerve damage and I don't know if it was really treated or not at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was the translation there where it says, "not treated" and question mark, that was a correct translation?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yeah, only a few misprints in the superficialis, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am just asking the reason that there is a question mark there is that you're not sure what--

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: --treatment he received?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let's go down to where it says "contractors" in 4 and 5. And your correction is that it should be contractions?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yeah, contractions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you explain what the PPD and the et cetera means --

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: PPD means the palm or pulp distance. And that is the difference between the pulp of the finger, the end of the finger and the distil palm crease. And this is then the PPD, the distance between the palm and the pulp over there. Normally you should get your hand with full flexion, it should be a PPD0 because you can get it right in the hand. If it is less, it means there is something still wrong, you cannot flex it completely. And here was a PPD of 2 and 4, so he cannot open his hand completely and there was a PPD -- 5 is one half, so it still opens up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. On the next line you have, "2PD, rather good." Would you explain that?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yeah, that is a two point discrimination. That means you can discriminate between one or two points. If you put one pin on a hand, you feel it as one pin. If you put two very close to each other at a certain time when it's coming too short, you cannot distinguish anymore between one point or two points. And there is a critical distance in between. If there is a lot of nerve damage completely, then you cannot distinguish with a very high number. But here it was still quite good.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you --

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: He could still feel quite all right, not too good, but not too bad too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you explain the cold intolerance in 4 and 5?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Cold intolerance means there has been some damage to the artery or to the nerve. And then you can react to the cold, if you put ice on the finger, for example, you get some pain in the fingers. That means cold intolerance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the local pressure and pain scar?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yeah, the local pressure means when you put your finger on the 5th finger, on the radial side, that means near the thumb, this side, there was local pain due to the damage of the nerve. And it was in the direction of the scar. There is a scar. Here was one scar and there was one scar. Scar tissue is still a bit solid and especially if the nerve is right under it, you get more pain if you press on it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were able to tell that by doing some pressing on his hand, correct?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Just local pressing and then he feels pain, he reacts on pain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of reaction did he have from the pain?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: He said it was painful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The last statement there where you have, "Compare measurements of Strength I and R," was that a reference to what more you could do if he were able to come to your hospital?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yeah, but first this was for my personal note, so it was a remembrance for myself and it means strength, left and right. Should be an L, the I. And, but you can measure, for example, pinch you can measure between the first and the second finger. And you can measure the force of a fist to the left and right side and you compare it and there is always some difference because you have left and right-handed people, but you have some idea. But it is mainly for these fingers and the fist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that you have equipment at your hospital that can do those kinds of tests, you just were not able to do those tests at the detention centre, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yeah, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would like to reurge and ask the Court to admit this report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We could admit it, but you have not indicated the purpose of the examination itself. You haven't even asked him. Of why he examine him. You have no reasons for sending him to examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Certainly I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I called you and told you that I would like for you to testify here, I asked you to go and do an examination, correct?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of that examination? What did you think that -- why did you think that you would be doing that examination?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Oh, you asked me if it was possible to hold a stick and use violence with it for a substantial time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if a stick -- well, let me say, Your Honour, with that qualification, may I now ask that it be admitted into evidence with the corrections that he has made that "contractors" should say "contractions" and "superlicialis" should say "superficialis"? With those two corrections, Your Honour, may I ask that it be admitted into evidence, his report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: So it is admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is your report after examining the accused person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's my report. I wrote one for myself. This is translation of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, with the corrections, it represents exactly what you intended to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think there is another error on some of the translation. In the second last line of his report, "eventually in Leyenburg," if -- I think should be "when."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I asked him about the possibility of coming to the hospital and what other kinds of tests that they can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Look at the sentence, it doesn't read.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Doctor, are you comfortable --

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, this was just for my own as a rememberness because if you were there at the hospital for this lung function, then I go in the same time, do this -- palm reading of the hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would be comfortable exchanging if for when?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It's not part of his report, it's just to remind him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's not part of my report. You can just omit the line, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, he has stated everything that he examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you just a few specific questions. If a person with his hand injury held a stick in his hand and hit somebody, would he feel pain?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yeah, I think he will feel pain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if he held the stick with, perhaps, these three fingers and hit somebody, would there still be pain from the pressure on this 4th and 5th finger?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: I think you don't hold it this way. I think you hold a stick with all your fingers and it can still open it up and so he can hold it. But, still, you will have some pain over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: How comfortable would somebody with this defect be able to hold a stick and hit someone with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think you can still hold a stick with that, but it is very difficult to let off your grip because it is two fingers are impaired, three fingers are normal. The three fingers you can still hold it, but with five you hold it not very stable, I think. He will be handier with the other hand, of course. But it is his right hand. He can still hold it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We seem to be having some problems. Mr. Delalic's defence has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the defence of Mr. Zdravko Mucic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: The Defence of Hazim Delic has no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic is repeating that the Defence of Mr. Zdravko Mucic has no questions for this witness. There may be an error in my statement. I said the Defence of Mr. Delalic and this has not gone done in the transcript. The microphone is not on, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The microphone probably was not on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To make sure that it goes down in the transcript, my microphone doesn't seem to be working. I just wanted to say that the Defence of Mr. Delalic has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Cowles, you can proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Cowles

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Haeseker.

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Jim Cowles, I represent the Prosecution in this matter. Dr. Haeseker, did you ever review any past medical records of Mr. Landzo?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These include his hand injury records?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Based on your examination of Mr. Landzo's hand, I believe you told Ms. Boler that the 4th finger, the 4th digit is, in your words, all right to function?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: No, it was not completely all right to function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain then what you meant?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, I told here there is a PPD of the 4th finger of 2 centimetres. It means he cannot get the finger completely in the hand. It was not a complete normal function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he can't touch the palm?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: He can't touch the palm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever perform any test yourself on Mr. Landzo's hand or his ability to use his right hand?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Well, I just saw him over there in Scheveningen once only and I asked him to do all the functions, to show to me what the functions were and that's what I wrote down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no knowledge, of course, of the facts of case of what Mr. Landzo is alleged to have done in 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: I have not, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've never seen him hold, for instance, a baseball bat?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never seen him hold a rifle or carry a rifle?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen him carry any objects of any weight at all?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: He brought a ventilator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A what?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: He brought a ventilator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He carried that okay?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware that he served in the war in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: I am aware.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware that he was never discharged for any sort of medical disability?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he shook hands with you, in fact, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: He did, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Just one brief question, Your Honour. Re-examined by Ms. Boler

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Haeseker, Mr. Cowles asked you if -- you mentioned that he carried in a little ventilator, could you describe the size of that, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: It was a big fan on wheels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was able to be pushed on wheels?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: It was about this. It was on wheels, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall whether he pushed it with his right hand or his left hand?

utterances.speaker: Barry Haeseker
utterances.text: I am not sure any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: No further questions, I pass this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Haeseker, you've been quite helpful. This is all we have for you. You are discharged. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: The next witness is Dr. Lammers, Ernst Lammers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, kindly swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I ask the usher's assistance to give Dr. Lammers a copy of his CV and his report. And I have extra reports for the registry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Curriculum vitae D 55/4 and the report D 56/4. . Examined by Ms. Boler

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning -- I mean, good afternoon, Dr. Lammers, and thank you for coming here to testify. Let me ask you to begin by stating your name for the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: My name is Ernst Lammers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How are you currently employed?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Hospital Leyenburg in The Hague for about two years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your position there, what kind of position do you have there?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Pulmonary doctor, chest physician, a staff member.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of pulmonary problems do you treat?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: I treat every area of the pulmonary diseases in my hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe just a couple of those to the court?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: For instance, COPD, asthma, lung cancer, I think, the main issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you define a percentage of your practice to asthma and breathing difficulties?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Asthma and breathing difficulties will be about 70 -- 60 to 70 per cent of my practice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me back up and ask you a little bit about your education. Would you explain to the Court what your education is and your medical education?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: My background, about my medical education, I become a doctor in 1990. Did my study at Nijmegen for about seven years. I practised my study to become a chest physician for two years in Almelo, a hospital. I did study of internal diseases, internal medicine. And after two years in '92 I ended my study for four years in Enschede and where I developed to a chest physician. So I am a doctor now for about eight years, nine years, nine years already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, excuse me, I see from your CV that you also have faculty experience. Can you tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Faculty experience is, I think you mean that I have done some course in France, in Marseilles, for instance. That's a faculty where you have the ability to explore the lung with instruments and it's a specific way of doing treatment and to make diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page of your CV, it says bronchoavcolaire. Could you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's a way of, put some water in the lung and to examine the fluid which is prepared after this. And it gives you an impression about a disease of the lung, what kind of disease it is and about activity of the disease at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute ago you told me that you estimated approximately 60 to 70 per cent of your practice has to do with asthma and breathing?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Difficulties. Can you describe for me -- if I just had a very limited understanding of asthma, can you explain to me what asthma is?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Asthma is a disease where the lungs do have a reaction on, for instance, cold air, exercise, where the airways will constrict and where you have mostly an obstructed -- and problems with breathing out. And the patient, or the man will feel that as a shortness of breath. And it can be adduced also by medicine, for instance, aspirin. And mostly with exercise, if you were doing something that the airways will be constricted and that you have the feeling of shortness of breath. So the treatment of asthma is also to give medicines to open the airways, to breathe freely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do most asthma patients -- is this something that happens at birth or in childhood or can it just happen any time?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: It can happen any time. Mostly it's that asthma patients do have the problems from birth already. And also, a lot of people have allergy problems, which also start in -- at the birth age. And people, if they can have asthma later on, for instance, about 30 or 40 years old, mostly it's caused by smoking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When someone presents themselves to you in an emergency room situation, can you describe what an asthmatic reaction, or correct my terminology, but when someone must come because of their asthma to the emergency room, what kind of symptoms do they display?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
