utterances.text: If someone is coming to the emergency room with an attack of asthma, asthma, you have an enormous constriction of airways, so you have an enormous problem to breathe out because the air will stay in the lungs. That cause a lack of oxygen in the blood, so people, if there is an enormous lack of oxygen, they will get blue, blue colour, what you can see, for instance, at the nail, at the tongue and sometimes at the skin. They will have a lot of problems with the heart, frequency is enormous, about 200. They will have problems with not only the oxygen, but also the -- called the dioxides, which you normally breathe out. Which if there are no change in the asthma check by treatment, it is possible that a patient can be conscious, unconscious and it is necessary to put the patient on the intensive care and to assist him with the breathing with mechanical ventilation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this country, when you treat asthma patients, is there a certain percentage of that group that needs medication on a constant basis, or do the great majority need medication on a constant basis? How does the medication work?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: We split up the degree of asthma. You have very mild asthma and you have very severe asthma. People who have severe asthma or serious asthma, they always need medicine, everyday, every time. If you have very mild asthma, sometimes it's necessary to take medicine about once or twice a week. But I, as a chest physician in addition in hospital, I see people who use almost every day, the medicine for the asthma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please, let's go to the examination of Landzo and his history of asthma.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right, Your Honours. I understand the direction. I just was wanting to know how he treated asthma patients. But, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, that's not what you brought him here for.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Well, eventually I'll be asking him to -- and shortly I will be going into the questions directly as related to what he knows about my client, but that's obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's not why you invited him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: That's true, Your Honour, but since he was not there when Esad Landzo was little and he was not there during in war, then I felt I just needed to ask some general questions about asthmatic patients, but I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I first contacted you to come and testify at this tribunal, one of the things that I asked you to do was go to the UN Detention Centre and visit with Esad Landzo there, correct?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did so on June the 2nd of this year and also on June the 6th; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of your visit, you wrote a report to me, detailing what you found in that visit, correct?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you actually sent this report to me by e-mail and so there is no -- there was no translation from Dutch to English?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so if this was printed out on my computer, and you've had an opportunity to glance over it, is this exactly what you typed out and wrote to me?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so it's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You've not got it translated?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was not a need for it to be translated because he actually wrote the report in English and this is actually his writing of that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In English, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought you said it was in Dutch, that's why I asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: What I intended to say was there was no need for a translation from Dutch to English because he wrote it in English the first time he wrote it. Well, I don't know. Let me back that up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only report that you've given me was this report, exactly this one?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point, I would move that this report be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask him if he believes this is the report he wrote, and he can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I believe I did ask him if this was the report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Does he have it now?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I gave it to me with the usher's assistance. He does have it before him. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it the report that you sent to her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is the report I sent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I am going to take just a few minutes to go over some of the things that you put in your report which were then a reflection of the interview that you had with Mr. Landzo. Okay, let's go down to the part that says, "medical history."

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, any information that you got from this report, the majority of the information came directly from what Mr. Landzo told you, correct?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did I also show you a short report that I had from a hospital in his hometown of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say that he had chronic bronchitis from the age of three months. You gave a lot of testimony about asthma. So let me also ask you about the bronchitis and if you can just explain to me how bronchitis differs from asthma?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: It's very familiar to asthma, chronic bronchitis will say that the airways are not only constricting sometimes, but that the airways itself are constantly affected by, for instance, bacterias or viruses, where you have a thickening of the airways. And that's the reason why chronic bronchitis has the problem that the airways are more sensitive to influences on the airways where the result will be the restricting of the airways. So, the only difference is that asthma has not a chronic infection, infection of the airways and only the constriction in chronic bronchitis, the combination of these two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do lay people sometimes use interchangeably bronchitis and asthma?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do lay people sometimes interchange the two, say somebody has bronchitis or somebody has asthma? Are they ever used interchangeably to mean the same thing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In the same sense, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it interchangeable, yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For physicians, I am sure there are differences between the two things, correct?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they're in the same family of respiratory illnesses; is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me move down to where you discuss an allergy for dust, parrots and feathers and then you have in parenthesis, 1996. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's a test we do in the blood to see if people are allergic. Indeed, now it's dust, parrots and feathers, but we're also looking to other issues. But if there is an allergy, we know as physician that you can have a lot of problems if you have contact with these items because it will also cause the restriction of the airways.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does this indicate -- did Mr. Landzo tell you that he had a blood test to see what he might be allergic to in 1996?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yeah, it is possible that -- yeah, you can see that in the blood test, to see if someone is -- has allergy. I didn't see the result of the test, but that's what he said and this is something we do to examine the asthma patients or bronchitis patients, what the cause is of their complaints of asthma and bronchitis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. In the family history, you've mentioned that his mother's father had asthma. Is it common that asthma runs in a family?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next thing is history and you've got, "Last ten years not so many complaints of bronchia and asthma." Did he tell you much about the number of complaints he had as a young person?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yes, a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recall what types of complaints he discussed, his treatment as a young person?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: His treatment, yeah, were treatments we don't know here in my country or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the ways in which he was treated that he discussed with you --

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- that's not the way you would do it here?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give me a comparison of these types of treatment as to what you would do now?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yeah. What we do now is treat with medicine to open the airways, to prevent the constriction of the airways. And the other treatment of medicine is what I told was that if the airways are affected chronic, they are hypersensitive, and we give medicine to press down the chronic infection of the airways, so that the hypersensitivity will disappear. And that you have as a patient not the problems you normally have the restrictions of the airways, for instance, if you have contact with parrots or if you're doing exercises or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the next statement that said he sometimes visited the hospital twice a day. Is that correct, twice a day?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yes, he told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you how long that intensity of treatment continued?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That was not really clear because there were problems to know what they really did at the hospital. But a lot of medicine you can give to asthma will only work for a few hours, so it's possible that if you have problems you can have medicine and a few hours later you will have again the same problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned an injection here, is that -- you treat by injection?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's only a part of the patients we treat with injection. If we have not any possibility to give the medicine in the airways, then we give injection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say give the medicine in the airways, do you mean by --

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: By breathing in, by the patient himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me also ask you about the word "intravenous" that immediately follows injection. Were those two words meant to go together just like a shot, or do you mean some kind of drip that stays in your vein for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: No. Just an injection, just after he get the medicine, the needle will get out. It's not something which stayed for some hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You also mention a paper being in pig grease on his chest, could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's something I never heard before and I can't find it in any paper anywhere else where this is treatment of asthma or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you about why he had to have that?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: He had to have that because of his shortness of breath. Yeah, I can't imagine what it will do, only that it will smell and maybe cause more severe asthma than it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you who arranged for him to have that treatment? Who did that?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: His family, his mother?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was not something that was done in the hospital, this was a home remedy, correct?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also discussed his shortness of breath at night. If he had had adequate medication, is this something that could have been controlled?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: To have problems at night will say anything about the degree of asthma. If he has problems of shortness of breath at night, mostly we have to do with asthma. And, yes, indeed, we have now about three to four years medicine to prevent the shortness of breath at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did I understand you to say that that medicine has only been available three or four years or that's the length of treatment?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: It's not that we have the medicine three or four years that we only now can treat the shortness of breath at night, but it is an expression of the degree of asthma where we have these medicine as an addition of the regular medicine we have. And then, if people have problems at night, some have -- if they use this medicine, are out of -- you know, shortness of breath at night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to telling you the problems that he had as young person, did he also talk with you about the problems he had during the war because of his asthma?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he -- I see in your report that he -- that you wrote that he couldn't properly walk because he was restricted by his shortness of breath. Can you explain what is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: I meant that the complaints he had and to know what severe asthma is, then is exercise very difficult to do, and then you can have a lot of problems with just only walking. If you have problems with walking, now then, you must have severe asthma at that moment because when I talked about degrees of asthma, if you have mild asthma, you can walk. Only if you do a lot of exercises, then you maybe have a little shortness of breath. But if you normally walk and you have already shortness of breath, you must have severe asthma. So it's an indication about the way the asthma was at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned Ventilin tablets, what are Ventilin tablets?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: It's a medicine to open the airways and which will, about three to four hours work. And -- a medicine which we used here in the Netherlands about ten, fifteen years ago, where you have a lot of side effects because it must be -- have to be working in the lungs and not in the body and if you take tablets, it will be all in the body and you have a lot of -- yeah, side effects. Ventilin is only medicine to give a widening of your airways in three or four hours and then it's finished. But it is not a way of treatment of asthma it should be. It's only -- you can -- similar is if you have a headache, you take aspirin, you don't treat the cause, you only treat the pain for a few hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then mention intravenous injections again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is this all about? If he has examined the accused and from the stories he gave him, asthma was consistent with that story. What are you posing about the treatment?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask some questions about how Mr. Landzo was treated during the war and what types of problems he conveyed the doctor and what types of breathing problems he had at that time. And that's why I was going into this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can he testify to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: All right, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Mr. -- Did Mr. Landzo tell you whether he was a smoker or a non-smoker?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Non-smoker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Briefly explain to me the problems that he may still be having with his breathing while he is with his asthma while he is in detention. Did you all discuss that?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yes, I discussed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he being treated properly here?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yes, he is being treated properly, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. On the next page, there are just some things that I really don't understand, can you take just a minute to explain.

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yeah, I will explain that. I brought an instrument, a measure instrument into the prison to have an impression about the obstruction of the airways. The obstruction of the airways is a measurement to see if we have to do with an obstructive lung disease and asthma or chronic bronchitis is an obstructive lung disease. And the numbers which I mention here in this report, if you then compare what is the reference numbers, it's about 70 per cent of the reference numbers he should be have. So we can say that because I measured six times in two different days, that we have to do here with chronic obstructive disease. And the diagnosis, asthma is because also of his medical history.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In conclusion, toward the bottom of your report, you state that his lung function shows there is a chronic obstruction of his airways. Is this chronic obstruction of his airways, is that asthma, is that bronchitis or?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Chronic obstructive disease can also be, for instance, emphysema. Yeah, that's another disease that's also familiar to it, to asthma, or chronic bronchitis. Asthma, if you have mild asthma, you can sometimes measure totally normal values of doing these exercises he did and if you see the values, then you can't talk about obstructive disease. You can only talk about chronic obstructive disease if you measure values which are constantly lower than the reference values. And that situation that you talk about chronic obstruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Granted it was just an examination that covered a period of two separate visits there, but based on what you saw and the breathing tests and the report that you read and what -- just all the things that you had available to you, is it your diagnosis that, in addition, to chronic obstruction, that this is a person who suffers from respiratory disease?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will rise and reassemble at 4.30, when cross-examination will continue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath. I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a couple. May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. Cross-examined by Mr. Moran

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran, and I represent a man named Hazim Delic. And I'm going to ask you a few questions and nobody is arguing with your diagnosis. I just want to clear some things up in my own mind. First, with the usher's help -- the usher is gone. If we could show the witness Exhibit D 6/3, I think it is. Doctor, have you seen one of those before?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a baseball bat. Given your examination of Mr. Landzo and your diagnosis, in your opinion in 1992, given his physical condition at that time, would it have been possible for him to strike a human body with that, say 200 times in a half hour, or would he likely have some kind of asthmatic attack?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: I cannot say that it isn't possible to do that and that it must be that he had an asthma attack. But the diagnosis say that it is almost the case if you have an exercise which is more than just walking. And you use no medicine at all, that you have a great chance that you have problems of shortness of breath, which will be progressive if the exercise will continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And hitting something fairly solid, that would be your opinion, the kind of exercise that could cause shortness of breath?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That could be. If you're not trained, it's an exercise which, indeed, can induce problems of shortness of breath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Doctor, given your evaluation of his medical condition in 1992 and 1993, could he function in the infantry in close combat in all likelihood?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: If you have this degree of asthma and you and if you don't use medicine at all, it isn't possible at any moment at any condition that you can do all exercise of everything a normal person can do, that's not possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So, in your opinion, it would be unlikely that he could function in close combat as an infantry soldier?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's very unlikely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How about doing hard labour, lifting -- unloading 20-ton trucks full of TVs, VCRs, stereos, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: What do you mean by that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could he do it, in all likelihood?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: It depends on the time that he has to do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's a fair answer and I won't follow it up because I don't have any further information on that. Last series of questions. I am going to change subjects completely. You're, of course, a physician and there is -- physicians have different specialities. You're in the a psychiatrist, of course?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or a psychologist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We know the evidence he has come to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree that asthma is a psychosomatic disorder and that difficulties with breath have to do with your relationship with your mother?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's not correct. Asthma is a disease which we have a subscript, we can prove it that if someone has asthma. If you have psychology problems, it can worsening the asthma. And we have what we see if people are under stress or have a relation problems or with work or doesn't matter, whatever. Mostly of the times, it will worsening the asthma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's not the cause of the asthma?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it would -- the stress would come -- or the asthma attack would come at the same time as the stress; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Stress can cause an asthma attack if there's asthma.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what I am getting at is that the two would tend to come together, the asthma attack and the stress?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: It's possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just because my mommy doesn't love me doesn't mean I am not going to have asthma, does it?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I pass the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Questions from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: May it please the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed Cross-examined by Mr. Cowles

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Dr. Lammers, my name is Jim Cowles and I represent the Prosecution in this matter. Good afternoon?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Lammers, isn't it true that you don't know any of the facts with which Mr. Landzo is charged or alleged to have committed during the course of 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't know or you can't say with any kind of medical assurety that if Mr. Landzo did hit someone with that bat a number of times, that he may or may not have developed an asthma attack on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: I can't say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you indicate in your report that, according to Mr. Landzo, that he got an asthma attack at a frequency of ten times a year?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's approximately less than once a month?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not exactly a chronic case of asthma, is it?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: You can have chronic asthma. An attack is just a worsening of the asthma and what you call an attack, but an attack is for someone else different than for another patient. And an attack is something what you feel shortness of breath and you can examine an attack if you are seeing a doctor to try to objective the problems of the asthma is at that moment. So if you say someone has ten times an attack, that can be for another maybe 40 or 50 times a year. An attack is the feeling that you have is shortness of breath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that's not what he told you, is it?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: He told me about many times that he felt there was an asthma attack. And what he told me was there was a severe asthma attack because when he told people that it was not so worse and he went to the hospital, he got a lot of medicine because it was, indeed, a severe attack because he was not saying that he was more ill than he was at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Well, he never told you that he was ever excused or disqualified or exempt from military duties because of asthma, did he?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Well, that he had problems with the activities in the army to do his job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was never excused or made exempt from military service because of asthma, was he, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: According to my information, was that sometimes he thought not to do activities what he was asked for because of his shortness of breath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Like what?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: I don't know what activities all, but one of the activities was that he had to go to the front and that walking with his luggage on his back was, yeah, a great problem for him because of his shortness of breath, because of his asthma and that was -- and he had to do that with the other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was never exempted or excused from military service, was he?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Not that I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he continued to go to the front and serve as a soldier and a military policeman throughout the war; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That can be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your -- in your conclusion, doctor, you make a statement, "I can't say which moment he can do some activities or he can't."

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain that a little bit. You can't say what activities he could or could not have done at a particular time?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: No, the reason I have written that is because if you suffer asthma in a period because it's winter, for instance, that's a period that my asthma patients have problems, doing exercises is much more difficult than, for instance, sometimes in the summer. So it depends on the degree of the asthma what is possible of exercises you can do at the moment. So I cannot say at what time he could do and what kind of exercise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or, any kind of physical activity?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yeah, sometimes it's not possible to do any physical exercise at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, in warm weather he could probably do a lot more physical activity than in cold weather without experiencing any asthma difficulty; wouldn't you say that's correct?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Sometimes it's possible because if you have a fair amount of asthma, then it can be the case, but if you have chronic asthma, then if the summer or winter, there will be certainly a difference, but not that you can say that in summer that you don't feel any shortness of breath if you're doing exercises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You indicate in your report of Mr. Landzo that in winter, and big differences of warm and cold?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's correct. That's a very familiar cause of problems of asthma patients.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you'd experience more asthma difficulty in cold whether, isn't that true, when you have physical exertion?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: Yeah, that's mostly the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In warm weather you'd have less asthma effects if you have physical exertion?

utterances.speaker: Ernst Lammers
utterances.text: That's mostly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. COWLES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I have some redirect questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, let me find out, you indicated in 1992 and 1993 there were breathing problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Landzo tell you how many of these incidences of asthmatic attack he had for that period.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had several asthma attacks in that period. I can't say now the number off my head because I don't have the report now. But, yeah, I want to say again that it's very important what is an asthma attack. For one person is an asthma attack about what he feel and another person will say, "It's going well and little shortness of breath and that's all." And it's very important what experience you have by yourself, what the shortness of breath is for yourself. But, what I told before, if you talk about an asthma attack, it must be, yeah, very severe because when he went to the hospital with his problems, it was a very severe attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Again, for a guard who stays outside watching over and in the open air, and not inside the house, is there a likely tendency that he could get the attacks more frequently than if he was in a different situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's possible because outside you're more influenced about the temperature, the humidity of the -- the climate where you are in. Also, dust or other allergy problems you can have, which will cause asthma problems, that's more often outside than inside a building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I have a few questions. Did he tell you that he had been taking medicines for his asthma since his childhood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He didn't have medicine which he had taken by himself. He had medicine given to him in a hospital when he has an asthma attack. And he didn't use any medicine at all by himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much. I think this is all we need from you. You may be discharged. Have we any other witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Sorry. Our next witness is Dr. Marco Lagazzi, who will have an Italian interpreter, and my understanding is that the interpreter will be present in the courtroom in the morning. And then we have four Bosnians who are arriving this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Your undertaking yesterday was that an interpreter would be available today and tomorrow. That was what you told the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I told the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, Mrs. McMurrey said the Italian interpreter would be available today, the 14th and 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Here's what happened. When the registry informed us that they would not be able to get an interpreter, an Italian interpreter until Wednesday, we called an Italian interpreter that we knew of in Amsterdam who was the women who translated the CVs and the reports that the Italian doctors gave us. And we were hopeful that she would be able to find interpreters for us. She was able to find two, but my instructions from the registry were that we needed three for different positions in the courtroom that I am not -- that I don't have any more information than that about. So, with that, we were not able to find our own, although we did spend a part of the afternoon yesterday trying to make some phone calls to see if it could be arranged. We -- you know, obviously the testimony just moved a little faster today than -- I figured there would be even more testimony in the morning before the Italian doctor would even begin, but that's not the way it turned out. So I apologise to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You don't have any other witness at the moment?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The Bosnians are arriving this evening and they'll be able to -- you know, they will be available for tomorrow and Dr. Lagazzi is scheduled to be the first witness up in the morning with the Italian interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, in the absence of any other witness, I think the Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble tomorrow morning at ten.
